explanations.explanation: Astonished is exactly the word Mark uses. The people weren't just nodding politely. They were stunned, because He taught “…as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.” I get a small version of that feeling when a whole tray comes out of the oven evenly golden.
That's not the word Mark gives us. He says the people were astonished at His teaching. The reason Mark gives is that He taught “…as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.”
Bored isn't the word, friend. Mark says the people were astonished at His teaching. That's about as far from bored as you can get. The reason Mark gives is that He taught “…as one who had authority…”

True, and the man says it loud. He cries out, “I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” This is a man with an unclean spirit, and he names Jesus right there in the synagogue. The words are out in the open for everyone to hear.
It's the other way around. The man with the unclean spirit says it plainly: “I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” He doesn't hint at it or mumble it. He cries it out in the synagogue.
That's the title he gives Jesus. He says, “I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” He also calls Him Jesus of Nazareth in the same cry. It's quite a thing to hear from that man, in that room.
That title does show up elsewhere. Two blind men call out “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” (Matthew 9:27). But the man in the synagogue doesn't say it. He says, “…the Holy One of God!”
That's a title people use for Jesus later. Pilate asks Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” (Mark 15:2). It isn't what this man says in Capernaum, though. He cries out, “…the Holy One of God!”

explanations.answer: Be silent and come out of him
explanations.explanation: Two commands, no waiting. Jesus says, “Be silent!” and then, “Come out of him!” He doesn't argue with the spirit or negotiate. He speaks, and the spirit has to listen.

explanations.answer: Tell Me your name right now
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask for a name here. He rebukes the spirit and says, “Be silent!” Then He says, “Come out of him!” Short and direct, with no questions.
No deadline is given, friend. Jesus doesn't say anything about the town or about tonight. He tells the spirit, “Be silent!” and “Come out of him!” That's all He says.

The text says the opposite. All the people were amazed and began to ask one another, “What is this? A new teaching with authority!” They had a LOT to say. Mark even records what they said to each other.

False. Mark says all the people were amazed and began to ask one another, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!” So they were talking about it. And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.

Commands is the word they use. They say, “He commands even the unclean spirits…” It fits what they just watched, because Jesus gave orders and the spirit came out. That's why they called it “A new teaching with authority!”
Obey is the other word they use. The people say the spirits “obey Him!” They saw it happen, so they didn't need much convincing. One command from Jesus, and the spirit came out.

Teaching is part of what amazed them, but it's not the word in this sentence. The people say, “He commands even the unclean spirits…” They had just watched Jesus give an order and get results. Commands is the word that fits.
Calls sounds close, but it's not what they say. They say Jesus “commands” the spirits. A call can be ignored, and these spirits obeyed. They did what He said.
The people never say they praise anything here. They say Jesus commands even the unclean spirits, and the spirits obey Him. Praise isn't in what they say. Commands and obey are the words.

explanations.answer: Through the whole region of Galilee
explanations.explanation: Mark says the news about Jesus spread quickly “…through the whole region of Galilee.” That's the whole region, not just one town. Quickly is Mark's word for it, too.

explanations.answer: Only around the town of Capernaum
explanations.explanation: It went much farther than that. Mark says the news spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee. Capernaum was just where it started.

explanations.answer: All the way down into Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Mark says the news spread quickly “…through the whole region of Galilee.” That's where it goes, and that's already a wide area.

Right, she's the one in bed with a fever. Mark says Simon's mother-in-law was sick, and they promptly told Jesus about her. This all happens at the home of Simon and Andrew. It's a quiet scene after the noise of the synagogue.

Jairus's daughter is a different story. Jairus, a synagogue leader, begs Jesus to help his little daughter (Mark 5:22-23). At Simon and Andrew's house, the one with the fever is Simon's mother-in-law.

That's another person Jesus helps, just not here. A centurion, an army officer, tells Jesus his servant is lying at home paralyzed (Matthew 8:5-6). In Simon and Andrew's house, the sick one is Simon's mother-in-law.
The text says otherwise. Mark says Simon's mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, and they “…promptly told Jesus about her.” Promptly means quickly, not a few days later.
False, and fast. Mark says Simon's mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, “…and they promptly told Jesus about her.” Nobody sat on the news. I wish my own messages got delivered that quickly.
True. Jesus goes to her, takes her by the hand and helps her up, and “The fever left her…” It's a simple moment. His hand reaches her and the fever is gone.
It's the other way around. Mark says, “The fever left her…” right after Jesus took her by the hand and helped her up. She went from sick in bed to up on her feet.
Serve is the word. Mark says the fever left her “…and she began to serve them.” Jesus had helped her up, and then she began to serve. Mark doesn't tell us anything beyond that.
Mark doesn't mention her thanking anyone, though it's easy to imagine. What he says is that the fever left her “…and she began to serve them.” Serve is the word in this verse.
Nobody is being warned here. With the fever gone, Mark says she “…began to serve them.” It's a calm scene, with a woman back on her feet and getting to work.

The whole town, just like Mark says. After sunset, people brought all the sick and demon-possessed to Jesus, “…and the whole town gathered at the door.” That's one doorway and a lot of neighbors. I've had a crowded kitchen, but never a crowded kitchen like that.
It was far bigger than a family gathering. Mark says “…the whole town gathered at the door.” One house, one door, and an entire town outside it.

The synagogue is where they were earlier that day. By evening, Jesus is at the house of Simon and Andrew. Mark says “…the whole town gathered at the door.” So the crowd shows up at the house, not the synagogue.

explanations.answer: Because they knew who He was
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Mark gives. Jesus “…would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.” He drove out many demons that night, and He didn't let them talk. Earlier in the synagogue, one spirit had already said, “…the Holy One of God!”

explanations.answer: Because the crowd was too loud
explanations.explanation: Mark doesn't say anything about noise. He says Jesus “…would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.” The reason has to do with who they knew Him to be.

explanations.answer: Because it was still the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Mark doesn't give that as the reason. He says Jesus would not allow the demons to speak “…because they knew who He was.” That's the only reason the text states.

Pray is it. Mark says Jesus got up early in the morning, while it was still dark, and went out to a solitary place to pray. The evening before, the whole town had gathered at the door. Mark doesn't tell us what He prayed. I think it says something that He starts His morning there.
Mark doesn't say rest. He says Jesus “…went out to a solitary place to pray.” Mark gives prayer as the reason He went there.
Simon and Andrew were fishermen (Mark 1:16), but that's not why Jesus goes out. Mark says He went out to a solitary place “to pray.” No nets involved.

That's what they say when they find Him: “Everyone is looking for You!” Simon and his companions had gone to look for Him. After the night before, with the whole town at the door, it's easy to see why they said it.
Nothing like that happens. The fever left Simon's mother-in-law and she began to serve them. When Simon and his companions find Jesus, they tell Him, “Everyone is looking for You!”

explanations.answer: The scribes want to see You
explanations.explanation: The scribes aren't mentioned in this part of the story. Simon and his companions say, “Everyone is looking for You!” That's all they report.

explanations.answer: Go on to the neighboring towns to preach
explanations.explanation: That's Jesus' answer. He says, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well…” Everyone was looking for Him in Capernaum, and His answer was to keep going. He says it's for others too.

explanations.answer: Go back to Capernaum to heal everyone
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says. Jesus says, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well…” He gives the neighboring towns as the plan. Healing everyone in Capernaum isn't part of His answer.

explanations.answer: Stay in this quiet place to pray longer
explanations.explanation: Jesus did go there to pray, but He doesn't say to stay. He says, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well…” Time to move on.

True. Jesus says it Himself: “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.” He gives a clear reason and then He goes. Mark says He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.

Jesus actually says it out loud. His words are, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.” So preaching is why He came, in His own words. Then He goes through Galilee doing exactly that.
